hook: Day 1: a library with no screen

slides.title: The first commit
slides.body: 24 files. No game, no engine, no window. Voxelyn started as a headless library for pixels and cellular simulation — and the list of non-goals was written as carefully as the list of goals: no input, no audio, no full physics, no ECS, no UI.

slides.title: Falling sand
slides.body: Grid2D packs every cell into 16 bits — material plus flags — chunked, with active and dirty marks. Only active chunks get stepped, so a world at rest costs almost nothing. The demo is that running: sand piling into a slope, water finding its level.

slides.title: And a green diamond
slides.body: The other demo: isometric projection, painter order by x+y, a red rectangle standing in for a character. Deliberately ugly. What was being tested was whether the draw order closes without seams between tiles — not whether the scene looked good.

slides.title: Three rules that held
slides.body: TypedArrays always. Zero allocation in the hot loop. Deterministic traversal, because a replay has to actually replay. Seven months and a full game later, all three still hold — and that's why the mine floor can be simulated cell by cell on a phone.

caption:
Seven months ago this was 24 files and no game.

I'm publishing the Voxelyn devlog retroactively — one post per pull request, in the order the work actually happened. This is day one: 18 January 2026.

Back then Voxelyn was a headless library. Surface2D over a Uint32Array. Grid2D, chunked, with active/dirty marks so a world at rest costs nothing to simulate. Deterministic traversals — row-major, bottom-up, morton. Its own RNG. Zero dependencies.

The original PRD spends more words on non-goals than goals: no window, no input, no audio, no engine, no ECS, no UI. Just the core.

The two images are the only demos that existed in that commit, and the first thing in the project that ever had a picture: sand and water falling through a 128x128 grid, and an isometric diamond with a red rectangle standing in for a character.

One detail I like: both screenshots were generated by actually building that January commit — checking it out into an isolated worktree, compiling it, and driving a headless browser to the frame. Not today's build pretending to be January. Every post in this series works that way, so you'll watch the HUD, the lighting and the art genuinely evolve week by week.

From here to an online co-op mining roguelike is seven months. I'm posting the whole path.
